title: Undeciphered: the Indus script
summary: Despite many attempts, the script of the Indus cities has not been deciphered. Its inscriptions are tiny, about five signs on average, and no bilingual text is known.
why: A major Bronze Age urban civilisation left thousands of inscriptions, yet not one word can be read.

notes.problem: Open question had no theories (schema requires 2-4).
'No named rulers attested' misreads the source, which says no rulers are known from outside records or myths that could anchor a decipherment.

question: What language did the Indus script write, and can it be read at all?
evidence: Over 400 principal signs (estimates up to about 694); texts average about five signs; no bilingual inscription; no rulers' names known from other records to test readings.
wouldSettle: A bilingual inscription, like the Rosetta Stone, or a much longer Indus text.

theories.name: Dravidian language
theories.idea: Argued by Knorozov, Parpola and Mahadevan, among others, as an early Dravidian language; no clear consensus has been established.

theories.name: Indo-Aryan language
theories.idea: S. R. Rao's Sanskritic readings were called subjective and unconvincing; the script lacks the inflectional endings Sanskrit would need.

theories.name: Munda language
theories.idea: A less popular proposal; early Munda vocabulary does not reflect Harappan culture, so its case is weak.

theories.name: Not a full writing system
theories.idea: Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004) argued the signs are non-linguistic; Rao et al. (2009) found language-like structure.
